situation: Mime is offered with five public Steel cards and full Joker slots.
options: Reroll and keep the current five Jokers.
Sell a replaceable Joker, reobserve, then consider Mime.
lesson: Mime can retrigger held Steel effects; surface the engine even when capacity makes purchase a separate later action.
reversal: Keep the current build when reliable output or economy matters more than draw-dependent held Steel.

situation: A free Hanging Chad is offered while Justice and enhanced scoring cards are public.
options: Skip and preserve the mature Joker lineup.
Sell, reobserve, and consider Chad for a first-card retrigger line.
lesson: Chad retriggers the first scoring card twice, so supported Glass or other scoring-card effects can justify a build transition.
reversal: Skip when no suitable first scoring card is available or the displaced Joker is essential for survival.

situation: Baron is offered with five public Kings, including a red-seal Steel King.
options: Reroll for a less draw-dependent upgrade.
Sell, reobserve, and consider Baron as held-card scaling.
lesson: Count public Kings and relevant seals before presenting Baron; multiple Kings make its held XMult route plausible, not guaranteed.
reversal: Decline when hand size, draw reliability, or a strong additive Joker makes holding Kings impractical.

situation: Constellation at X1 is offered beside an established Baseball engine and visible Planet plans.
options: Keep current flat Mult and interest.
Transition to an uncommon scaler and fund future Planet use.
lesson: Constellation starts weak but is uncommon for Baseball and grows on Planet use; treat it as a conditional investment.
reversal: Pass when there is no Planet budget or immediate scoring cannot absorb an X1 scaler.

situation: Hologram at X1 is offered with Baseball and a visible pattern of opening card-adding packs.
options: Reroll and retain current scoring.
Replace a flat Joker and commit to adding useful cards.
lesson: Hologram is an uncommon Baseball target and grows when cards are added, but X1 alone is not an immediate scoring upgrade.
reversal: Pass when added cards would dilute the deck or there is no budget to grow Hologram.

situation: Ramen is offered after the build has stabilized and can reduce discretionary discards.
options: Keep Cloud 9 income and Holographic Mult.
Sell Cloud 9, reobserve, then buy Ramen for XMult.
lesson: Ramen begins at X2 and loses X0.01 per discarded card; buying it should change later discard discipline.
reversal: Keep economy when survival still depends on frequent discards or the lost income funds stronger upgrades.

situation: A red-seal Steel card is public when Mime is offered.
options: Build around holding the sealed Steel card.
Keep playing it when its rank or hand shape is more valuable.
lesson: Mime retriggers held-card abilities and a red seal adds a card repetition; confirm the card can remain held.
reversal: Abandon the line when forced selection, debuff, or hand-size pressure prevents holding it.

situation: Baron is offered with only the normal or low public King count.
options: Buy and begin a King-duplication plan.
Prefer a reliable multiplier already supported by the deck.
lesson: Baron gives X1.5 for each held King, but low King density makes the payoff draw-dependent.
reversal: Take Baron when duplication, hand size, or a held-card retrigger already makes the direction coherent.

situation: Baron and Mime share a held-King or Steel plan.
options: Add more Baron-style held XMult.
Add more held-card repetitions through Mime or a copier.
lesson: Balance effect count against retrigger count using the cards actually held; neither Joker is universally the better copy target.
reversal: Favor the side that is currently scarcer after counting held effects, seals, and copy placement.

situation: Stuntman supplies chips while a held-card engine needs room for Kings or Steel.
options: Keep Stuntman for reliable chips.
Replace it to restore hand size for more held effects.
lesson: A held-card build should price Stuntman's hand-size reduction against its dependable chip contribution.
reversal: Keep Stuntman when chips are the bottleneck or the deck cannot reliably fill added held slots.

situation: A Glass face can be placed first among scoring cards with Photograph and Chad active.
options: Lead with the Glass face for repeated effects.
Preserve Glass and use a safer scoring card.
lesson: Glass gives X2, Photograph can give X2 on the first scoring face, and Chad repeats the first scoring card twice.
reversal: Avoid the line when the score is already sufficient or losing Glass would damage future survival.

situation: Several selected cards score, but only one has a strong enhancement or edition.
options: Place the supported card first physically.
Keep current order when another first-card effect dominates.
lesson: Chad repeats the first scoring card. Reordering the same physical cards can change the score; remap selected slots after the reorder.
reversal: Do not reorder when the candidate scorer shows no gain or a boss/order effect makes the result uncertain.

situation: Photograph is offered but the public deck has few or no face cards.
options: Buy and plan to add faces.
Pass for an engine supported by current cards.
lesson: Photograph needs the first played face card to score; its label alone is not evidence of reliable XMult.
reversal: Take it when face density, copying, or retriggers make a deliberate face-scoring plan credible.

situation: Blueprint can be positioned to copy Hanging Chad in a played-card engine.
options: Copy Chad for more first-card repetitions.
Copy a main multiplier instead.
lesson: Copy placement should follow the current scoring card and multiplier chain, not a fixed target rule.
reversal: Copy the main multiplier when first-card effects are weak, debuffed, or absent from the play.

situation: Brainstorm is owned with several compatible engines in different Joker positions.
options: Move the desired target to the leftmost slot.
Leave order when the current target is better.
lesson: Brainstorm copies the leftmost Joker if that Joker is compatible; it does not search onward for a compatible target.
reversal: Do not reorder when hidden Jokers or a boss prevents a reliable public comparison.

situation: Blueprint's immediate right neighbor changed after a purchase or boss shuffle.
options: Reorder toward the intended compatible target.
Keep order and accept the current target.
lesson: Blueprint copies the compatible Joker to its right; purchases and shuffles require a fresh target check.
reversal: Skip automatic reordering when the target is hidden or scorer coverage is unavailable.

situation: A face card can be selected as a non-scoring kicker while a numbered card forms the scoring hand.
options: Use the face only as a harmless kicker.
Choose a play where the face scores.
lesson: Ride the Bus resets on a scoring face; distinguish scoring cards from selected kickers.
reversal: Treat safety as uncertain with unsupported interactions or when Splash makes every selected card score.

situation: Shortcut or Four Fingers can make a Straight plan easier to draw.
options: Buy consistency and invest in Straight levels.
Keep a more reliable small-hand engine.
lesson: Shortcut permits rank gaps; Four Fingers reduces the required Straight length to four. Check the actual rank spread before committing.
reversal: Pass when the deck still cannot draw Straights reliably or the slot must supply immediate score.

situation: A play leaves only Spades and Clubs in hand.
options: Play off-colour cards to activate Blackboard.
Keep a valuable red-suit held card and lose Blackboard.
lesson: Blackboard gives X3 when every held card is a Spade or Club; evaluate the actual cards left behind.
reversal: Keep the red-suit card when its Steel, seal, or future value outweighs current Blackboard XMult.

situation: A suit-changing consumable can turn red-suit cards into Spades or Clubs for Blackboard.
options: Edit suits toward a more reliable held-black condition.
Use the consumable for another hand or save it.
lesson: Deck edits can improve Blackboard reliability, but a visible target and legal phase are required.
reversal: Avoid the edit when it breaks a stronger flush, suit, or boss plan.

situation: Runner has accumulated chips, but the deck is becoming less reliable at making Straights.
options: Keep playing Straights to continue growth.
Preserve the banked chips and pivot the hand plan.
lesson: Runner keeps its accumulated chips; future growth requires playing another Straight.
reversal: Keep committing when Straight consistency and hand levels remain the best route.

situation: Ancient Joker names a suit that the current public hand or deck may not support.
options: Build the scoring hand around the named suit.
Use a reliable hand and forgo its trigger.
lesson: Ancient Joker rewards scoring cards of its current suit, so judge the visible suit rather than generic Flush strength.
reversal: Follow the target when enough scoring cards of that suit are available without breaking the hand.

situation: Bloodstone is supported by visible Hearts, but its scoring-card triggers are random.
options: Play a Heart-heavy scoring hand.
Choose the steadier available line.
lesson: Bloodstone gives scoring Hearts a chance to add X1.5 Mult; treat the payoff as stochastic rather than guaranteed.
reversal: Prefer the steady line when the blind cannot tolerate a missed trigger.

situation: A Standard Pack can add a card while Hologram is owned.
options: Add a useful card and grow Hologram.
Skip a weak card to protect deck consistency.
lesson: Hologram grows when a playing card is added, but growth does not make every offered card a good deck edit.
reversal: Add the card when its rank, enhancement, seal, or edition supports the main engine.

situation: A Planet for the main hand is available while Constellation is owned.
options: Use it for both hand level and Constellation growth.
Save money or choose a different pack card.
lesson: Planet use grows Constellation by X0.1 and can also level the relevant hand; verify the Planet matches the actual build.
reversal: Skip when economy or a stronger pack choice outweighs the combined incremental growth.

situation: No discard has been used this round and Burnt Joker can level the first discarded poker hand.
options: Discard the hand family intended for leveling.
Save the discard for draw quality.
lesson: Burnt Joker levels only the first discarded poker hand each round, so the first discard determines its growth target.
reversal: Use the discard for survival when shaping the named hand would make the round unsafe.

situation: Several legal plays clear, but only one names the hand intended for long-term leveling.
options: Play the target family and hold the Blue Seal.
Take the higher immediate score from another family.
lesson: Blue Seal value depends on the hand actually played; align it with the build rather than any sufficient hand.
reversal: Choose immediate score when the target-family line risks losing the blind.

situation: Card Sharp is active after the same poker hand has already been played this round.
options: Repeat the family for X3 Mult.
Change family for a stronger base hand or boss constraint.
lesson: Card Sharp gives X3 only after that poker hand was already played this round; first-hand and repeat-hand scores differ.
reversal: Change families when the repeated hand is illegal, debuffed, or cannot meet the target.

situation: A discard advances Yorick toward its next permanent XMult increase, but also spends draw control.
options: Advance Yorick with a safe discard.
Keep the discard for hand completion.
lesson: Yorick rewards a cumulative number of discarded cards; progress can be deferred when the current round needs draw control.
reversal: Spend the discard when the remaining hands and deck make the clear secure.

situation: Ramen is active and a discard could improve the next hand.
options: Avoid the discard and preserve XMult.
Discard because draw quality or survival is worth X0.01.
lesson: Ramen loses X0.01 per discarded card, so discard value must exceed a visible persistent scoring cost.
reversal: Discard freely when the current hand cannot clear or the better draw protects the run.

situation: A relevant Joker is visible but all normal Joker slots are occupied.
options: Sell a chosen Joker, settle, then reassess the offer.
Keep the lineup and preserve money.
lesson: A full slot hides an immediate buy action, not the strategic offer; selling and buying are separate decisions with a fresh observation.
reversal: Do not sell when the offer may disappear, capacity is uncertain, or the current Joker is needed for the next blind.

situation: A visible Jack can be discarded for Hit the Road during the current round.
options: Discard the Jack for temporary XMult.
Keep it for the scoring hand or future draw shape.
lesson: Hit the Road gains XMult for discarded Jacks and resets after the round, so this is a current-round payoff.
reversal: Keep the Jack when it is essential to the scoring hand or the temporary gain is unnecessary.

situation: Buying a supported scaler would cross an interest threshold.
options: Preserve the economy floor.
Spend now for a coherent scoring transition.
lesson: Compare known interest loss with the engine's conditions and next-blind need; neither saving nor spending is universally correct.
reversal: Preserve cash when the offer starts inactive or the current build already clears comfortably.

situation: The visible Plant debuffs face cards while the build uses Photograph or held Kings.
options: Reroll or adapt away from faces.
Proceed if non-face engines still clear.
lesson: The Plant can suppress a face engine; evaluate Photograph or Baron with the visible boss rather than deck counts alone.
reversal: Keep the engine when the boss is disabled or other scoring layers make the blind safe.

situation: A Planet matches the hand repeatedly used by Card Sharp and the current plan.
options: Level the established hand.
Choose economy, deck editing, or a speculative family.
lesson: Concentrating levels in the hand actually played improves its base before later multiplier effects.
reversal: Diversify when a boss blocks the main family or the deck has clearly transitioned to another hand.

situation: Smeared Joker can make red or black cards cooperate in Flush hands.
options: Build around easier Flush draws.
Keep the slot for score and pursue another hand.
lesson: Smeared treats Hearts and Diamonds as one suit, and Spades and Clubs as one suit. Consistency alone does not supply scaling.
reversal: Pass when Flush levels and scoring support are weak or a visible suit-debuff boss undermines the plan.

situation: Castle names a discard suit, and cards of that suit are visible.
options: Discard matching cards to add chips.
Save them for the scoring hand.
lesson: Castle gains chips only from discarded cards of its current suit; check the visible target before spending a discard.
reversal: Keep matching cards when they are needed to form the winning hand.

situation: Perkeo can copy a held consumable when leaving the shop.
options: Hold the consumable and leave to copy it.
Use or sell it before leaving.
lesson: On leaving the shop, Perkeo randomly copies one held consumable as Negative; manage the possible targets. Negative copies bypass normal capacity.
reversal: Use the original first when its immediate effect is more valuable than another copy.

situation: DNA or Death can duplicate a rank already central to a Five of a Kind plan.
options: Copy the supported rank or enhanced card.
Preserve hand economy and current consistency.
lesson: DNA copies a single-card first hand; Death converts one selected card into another, so target identity and order matter.
reversal: Do not force duplication when the setup hand risks the blind or the target cannot be selected legally.

situation: Face cards can score with Triboulet, Sock and Buskin, or Photograph visible.
options: Build a face-scoring retrigger chain.
Retain a non-face engine resistant to face debuffs.
lesson: Triboulet gives scoring Kings and Queens X2; Sock retriggers faces; Photograph rewards the first scoring face.
reversal: Pivot when face density is low or face debuffs disable the engine; hidden cards add uncertainty rather than automatically disabling it.

situation: Money is near Vagabond’s threshold before a scoring hand.
options: Stay at or below the threshold to create Tarot.
Keep or earn more money for shop economy.
lesson: Vagabond creates a Tarot after a scoring hand only when money is at or below its threshold and capacity allows.
reversal: Favor economy when deliberately staying poor costs more than the Tarot generation is worth.

situation: To the Moon, Rocket, or Business Card offers economy instead of immediate scoring.
options: Invest in income for later shops.
Buy scoring needed for the next blind.
lesson: To the Moon improves interest, Rocket pays and grows after bosses, and Business Card can pay on scoring faces.
reversal: Prefer immediate score when the run cannot safely wait for the economy to repay its slot and cost.

situation: Scoring 2s can trigger both Wee Joker growth and Hack retriggers.
options: Build the scoring hand around supported 2s.
Use a stronger hand without forcing low ranks.
lesson: Wee Joker gains chips from scoring 2s, while Hack retriggers ranks 2 through 5; their overlap makes public 2 density relevant.
reversal: Pivot when too few low ranks can score reliably or a boss debuffs the line.

situation: Observatory is owned and a Planet matching the played hand can remain held.
options: Hold the matching Planet for XMult.
Use it now to level the hand and free capacity.
lesson: Observatory makes a held matching Planet give X1.5; compare repeated held value with permanent hand leveling.
reversal: Use the Planet when capacity, immediate base score, or another consumable matters more.

situation: Madness is considered with Eternal Jokers or expendable slots before a non-boss blind.
options: Build a protected shell around Madness growth.
Keep several ordinary Jokers and avoid random destruction.
lesson: Madness gains XMult and destroys another Joker on Small or Big Blind selection; Eternal status changes the destruction risk.
reversal: Pass when key non-Eternal Jokers cannot be protected or upcoming growth opportunities are too few.

situation: Midas Mask and Vampire can interact on scoring face cards, but Joker order controls whether new Gold is consumed immediately.
options: Order Midas before Vampire for same-play feeding.
Order Vampire before Midas to leave new Gold cards.
lesson: Midas makes scoring faces Gold; Vampire removes scoring-card enhancements for growth. Vampire removes enhancements, not seals.
reversal: Preserve Gold or another enhancement when its card value matters more than immediate Vampire growth.

situation: Two or more poker hands are tied for most played while Obelisk is owned or offered.
options: Play a hand below the tied leaders.
Skip Obelisk and continue a leading hand.
lesson: Obelisk resets on a hand tied for most played; a safe pivot must be below every current leader.
reversal: Take a leading hand when it is required to clear or no lower-count hand is reliable.

situation: Low-rank cards can support Hiker, Wee Joker, Fibonacci, or Hack.
options: Retrigger and permanently grow supported low ranks.
Favor higher ranks or another hand engine.
lesson: Hiker adds permanent chips, Wee grows from scoring 2s, Fibonacci rewards A/2/3/5/8, and Hack retriggers 2 through 5.
reversal: Pass when supported ranks are sparse, debuffed, or cannot form the chosen scoring hand.

situation: A small or big blind is selectable and carries a tag that only a skip can claim.
options: Play the blind for its cash reward and the shop that follows.
Skip the blind and take the tag now.
lesson: Skipping forfeits only that blind's cash reward and its shop; the ante target is unchanged, so skipping pays most on early small blinds and on big blinds you cannot profitably shop after.
reversal: Play the blind when the reward plus shop is what the build needs, when money is short, or when a later blind will be harder without one more shop.

situation: The selectable blind carries a Negative Tag.
options: Play the blind and keep the reward.
Skip, then buy the first base-edition shop Joker.
lesson: Negative Tag makes the next base-edition shop Joker Negative and free, and Negative adds a Joker slot, so its value is a permanent slot plus a free Joker, not the Joker itself.
reversal: Skip it when no shop follows before the tag would be used, or when the likely shop Jokers are ones you would not keep in a permanent slot.

situation: The selectable blind carries a Rare Tag.
options: Play the blind for cash.
Skip and take a free Rare Joker in the next shop.
lesson: Rare Tag adds a free Rare Joker to the next shop, which is strong when a Joker slot is free but wasted if every slot is committed and nothing is worth selling.
reversal: Play the blind when slots are full of scaling Jokers, since a random Rare is not automatically better than a grown Joker.

situation: The selectable blind carries a Charm Tag.
options: Play the blind and buy Tarots later.
Skip and open the free Mega Arcana pack.
lesson: Charm Tag opens a free Mega Arcana pack, five Tarots choose two; it is worth most when the deck still needs shaping and consumable slots are free to hold what you pick.
reversal: Prefer the blind when the deck is already shaped and money, not Tarots, is the constraint.

situation: The selectable blind carries a Double Tag.
options: Skip now and let Double copy whatever the next tag is.
Play this blind and wait for a better tag to double.
lesson: Double Tag copies the next tag taken, unless that tag is another Double; its value is entirely the value of the tag you pair it with, so the pairing decides whether skipping is worth it.
reversal: Take the blind instead when the next visible tags are weak, since a doubled weak tag is still weak.

situation: The selectable blind carries an Investment Tag.
options: Play the blind for its immediate reward.
Skip and collect $25 after the next boss is defeated.
lesson: Investment Tag pays $25 only once the boss blind is defeated, so it is deferred income that also raises the interest base if the money is still held at cash out.
reversal: Skip it when survival against the boss is doubtful, because a payout conditional on beating the boss is worth nothing if the run ends there.

situation: The selectable blind carries a Voucher Tag.
options: Play the blind and take the single shop voucher.
Skip so the next shop offers an extra voucher.
lesson: Voucher Tag adds one more voucher to the next shop; it converts money into choice, so it pays when you can afford $10 vouchers and are hunting a specific one such as Telescope.
reversal: Play the blind when money is too tight to buy any voucher, since a second unaffordable offer changes nothing.

situation: The selectable blind carries a Coupon Tag.
options: Play the blind and pay normal shop prices.
Skip so every card and pack in the next shop is free.
lesson: Coupon Tag sets every shop card and booster to $0 for that one shop, so its value scales with how many slots you can actually use and with keeping money for rerolls, which stay paid.
reversal: Play the blind when Joker and consumable slots are full, because free items you cannot hold are worth little.

situation: Death is held and two hand cards could be selected.
options: Convert a weak card into a copy of a key card.
Keep the deck as it is and save the slot.
lesson: Death needs exactly two selected cards and copies the rightmost onto the other, so ordering decides which card survives; it duplicates enhancement, seal and edition along with rank and suit.
reversal: Do not use it when the sacrificed card is a seal, Steel or suit the build still needs, or when narrowing the deck hurts a straight or flush plan.

situation: Strength is held and low or off-plan ranks are visible in hand.
options: Raise up to two cards one rank toward the build.
Save it for a later, more valuable target.
lesson: Strength raises up to two selected cards by one rank and an Ace wraps back to 2, so it builds pairs and Kings for held-card engines but can break a straight it was meant to complete.
reversal: Skip it when the current ranks already form the intended hand, or when wrapping an Ace would cost a high-card or straight line.

situation: The Hanged Man is held and the deck carries cards that never score.
options: Destroy up to two dead cards to thin the deck.
Keep the deck size and preserve draw volume.
lesson: The Hanged Man permanently destroys up to two selected cards, which raises the chance of drawing the cards that matter, but every removal also lowers the number of cards left for hand-size and held-card conditions.
reversal: Keep the cards when the build needs bodies in hand, such as Blackboard or held-Steel plans, or when the removed suit is still part of a flush.

situation: Judgement is held and Joker capacity is in question.
options: Use it now while a Joker slot is free.
Hold it until the build knows which slot to spend.
lesson: Judgement creates one random Joker and does nothing without a free Joker slot, so it is a lottery ticket whose value depends on having room and on how replaceable the current worst Joker is.
reversal: Do not clear a working Joker to make space, because the created Joker is random and may be worse than what was sold.

situation: The Fool is held after some Tarot or Planet has already been used this run.
options: Use a high-value Tarot or Planet first, then The Fool.
Use The Fool immediately.
lesson: The Fool copies the last Tarot or Planet used and never copies another Fool, so its value is set by the previous use; sequencing an expensive Planet or a build-defining Tarot first doubles that effect.
reversal: It does nothing when a consumable slot is not free, and it is wasted right after a cheap or off-plan consumable.

situation: The Hermit is held while money is being decided in the shop.
options: Spend first and use The Hermit afterwards.
Use The Hermit before spending.
lesson: The Hermit doubles current money but adds at most $20, so it pays in full only when at least $20 is held; using it before purchases and after reaching $20 is strictly better than using it while broke.
reversal: It is worth nothing at $0 and gives less than its cap below $20, so it is not a reason to keep a consumable slot occupied indefinitely.

situation: Temperance is held alongside several bought Jokers.
options: Cash it now for the current total sell value.
Hold it until the Joker line is more expensive.
lesson: Temperance pays the combined sell value of all owned Jokers, capped at $50; it grows as expensive Jokers are added and pays nothing meaningful with a cheap or empty Joker line.
reversal: Do not delay past the cap chasing more, and do not keep it over a Tarot the build actually needs.

situation: Cryptid is held with one clearly best card in hand.
options: Copy the best scoring or held card twice.
Save it until a better target exists.
lesson: Cryptid adds two copies of one selected card, including its enhancement, seal and edition, so it multiplies an engine card rather than adding a random one; it also dilutes the deck by two cards.
reversal: Hold it when no card is worth tripling yet, since the extra copies also make other draws less likely.

situation: Immolate is held while money is the immediate constraint.
options: Take $20 and lose five random cards in hand.
Keep the deck intact and find money elsewhere.
lesson: Immolate pays $20 and destroys five random cards from hand, not chosen ones, so it trades unpredictable deck loss for cash; seals, Steel and enhanced cards can be among the five.
reversal: Refuse it when the build depends on specific held cards, or when $20 does not actually buy the missing piece.

situation: Ankh is held with more than one Joker owned.
options: Use it to duplicate a Joker.
Keep the current Joker line intact.
lesson: Ankh copies one random Joker and destroys every other non-eternal Joker, and the copy loses a Negative edition; with several useful Jokers it is far more likely to delete the build than to double it.
reversal: It becomes reasonable only when the line is effectively one Joker that matters, so the random pick cannot miss.

situation: Wraith is held and a Rare Joker would help the build.
options: Use it while money is already spent.
Use it now and lose the current balance.
lesson: Wraith creates a random Rare Joker and then sets money to $0, so its real price is everything held; using it just after spending, and before cash out rebuilds interest, is much cheaper than using it while rich.
reversal: Do not use it when the held money is needed for a known purchase or for interest, and note the Rare Joker is random, not chosen.

situation: Ectoplasm is held and a Joker without an edition is owned.
options: Take a Negative Joker and lose hand size.
Keep hand size and find the slot elsewhere.
lesson: Ectoplasm makes a random editionless Joker Negative, gaining a Joker slot, and permanently reduces hand size; the penalty grows with each use in the run, at one, then two, then three cards.
reversal: Avoid it when hand size carries the build, such as held-card, Blackboard or flush plans, and when the random target could be a Joker you would not want locked in.

situation: The Soul is available from a pack or already held.
options: Make room and take the Legendary Joker.
Take another card from the pack.
lesson: The Soul creates a Legendary Joker, which needs a free Joker slot to appear; the five Legendaries differ sharply, so it is a strong but not automatic upgrade over a grown scaling Joker.
reversal: Pass when every slot holds a scaling engine and the Legendary would not beat what is sold to make room.

situation: Black Hole is available while the played hand family is still moving.
options: Level every poker hand once.
Prefer a Planet that levels one hand further.
lesson: Black Hole raises every poker hand by one level, which is worth more than a single Planet only while the build still switches families or plays several hands; a committed one-hand plan gains more from repeated Planets.
reversal: Prefer targeted Planets once the most-played hand is fixed, and remember Observatory rewards holding the matching Planet, not Black Hole.

situation: A voucher is offered for $10 while money is also needed for Jokers.
options: Buy the voucher for a permanent effect.
Keep the money for the shop and interest.
lesson: Vouchers are permanent and one per shop, so scaling ones come first: Telescope then Observatory, then Hone or Glow Up, then shop width and reroll cost, then capacity, then economy; Blank does nothing this run.
reversal: Skip the voucher when $10 breaks an interest step or blocks the Joker that keeps the run alive, since the offer usually returns in a later shop.

situation: Telescope is offered while one poker hand dominates the plan.
options: Buy it and commit to that hand family.
Stay flexible across hand families.
lesson: Telescope makes the first card of every Celestial pack the Planet for your most-played hand, so it converts pack luck into reliable levels only once one family is clearly most played.
reversal: It is weak while hands are still split across families, and worthless if Celestial packs are not being opened.

situation: Observatory is offered, which requires Telescope to have been redeemed.
options: Buy it and keep matching Planets in hand.
Spend the money on scoring or economy instead.
lesson: Observatory turns each held Planet into X1.5 Mult for its own hand type, so it pays only if consumable slots are kept free to hold those Planets rather than using them immediately for levels.
reversal: It is poor when consumable slots are always full or when Planets are consumed on sight for hand levels.

situation: Hone or Glow Up is offered while Jokers are still being bought.
options: Buy it to raise the edition rate.
Buy scoring or economy instead.
lesson: Hone makes Foil, Holographic and Polychrome twice as common and Glow Up four times; the payoff is spread over every future shop card, so it needs enough remaining antes and shop volume to repay $10.
reversal: Skip it late in the run, or when few further purchases are planned, because it changes nothing already owned.

situation: Overstock is offered while rerolls are being used to find a specific Joker.
options: Buy Overstock for a wider shop.
Keep rerolling the current shop width.
lesson: Overstock adds one card slot to every future shop, which raises the chance a given reroll shows what you want and so lowers the effective cost of searching.
reversal: It is weak when money is too tight to buy from the shop at all, since more choices do not help without cash.

situation: Reroll Surplus is offered in a build that rerolls often.
options: Buy it to cut every future reroll by $2.
Keep the $10 for purchases.
lesson: Reroll Surplus lowers reroll cost by $2 for the rest of the run, so it repays $10 only after about five rerolls; it fits searching builds and is dead money in builds that leave shops early.
reversal: Skip it when the plan is to buy the first workable option rather than search, or when the run is close to ending.

situation: Blank or Antimatter is offered for $10.
options: Buy it as a permanent upgrade.
Treat Blank as a non-purchase.
lesson: Antimatter permanently adds a Joker slot and is worth $10 whenever the build wants a sixth Joker; Blank has no in-run effect at all and only progresses the unlock for Antimatter in later runs.
reversal: Even Antimatter is a poor buy when the current Jokers do not fill the slots already available.

situation: Seed Money is offered while money is regularly held above $25.
options: Buy it and start banking past $25.
Keep spending at the $25 cap.
lesson: Seed Money raises the interest cap from $5 to $10 per cash out, which needs $50 held to pay in full; it repays $10 in two capped rounds but only if the money is actually held rather than spent.
reversal: It is wasted when money is spent down each shop, and near the last ante it cannot repay itself.

situation: Money Tree is offered after Seed Money has been redeemed.
options: Buy it and bank toward $100.
Convert money into scoring now.
lesson: Money Tree raises the interest cap to $20 per cash out, requiring $100 held for the full amount; it is an economy engine that only matters when the run will last several more antes.
reversal: Prefer scoring when the next blind is already in doubt, because uncapped interest is worthless if the run ends first.

situation: Grabber or Paint Brush is offered while blinds are being cleared narrowly.
options: Buy the permanent capacity increase.
Buy scoring or economy instead.
lesson: Grabber adds a hand every round and Paint Brush adds a card to hand size; both directly raise survival, and Paint Brush also helps held-card engines and hand-size dependent Jokers.
reversal: Skip Paint Brush when hand size was deliberately reduced for a build, and skip Grabber when hands are not the limiting resource.

situation: Director's Cut is offered while a hostile boss blind is upcoming.
options: Buy the ability to reroll one boss per ante.
Adapt to whatever boss appears.
lesson: Director's Cut allows one boss reroll per ante for $10 each time, so its real cost is $10 plus $10 per use; it is insurance against a boss that disables the single mechanism the build depends on.
reversal: It is poor when the build survives most bosses, since the money buys nothing on the antes where no reroll is needed.

situation: A Glass face card sits in hand with Photograph, Hanging Chad and a copier, and a safer non-Glass card could take the first slot instead.
options: Hold the Glass card back and lead with a plain high card.
Lead with the Glass face and accept the break roll.
lesson: Only the first played card is retriggered, so Glass and Photograph compound there: the recorded Ace-led Steel flush scored 764,127 where the same hand led by a face and holding the Glass Ten scores 1,222,760,448.
reversal: Lead a plain face when the blind already falls to the safer hand and that Glass card is the last one the engine can still use.

situation: A Glass-led retrigger engine is carrying the run and the shop can still add or convert cards.
options: Bank the money and keep rerolling for another Joker.
Spend on Glass supply: Justice, Strength on a Glass Ten, or a Standard pack.
lesson: Every retrigger rolls the Glass one-in-four break, so the lead card is consumed fastest: the recorded deck fell from seven Glass cards to four across two blinds and lost both Glass faces before the boss.
reversal: Stop buying Glass supply when the remaining blinds fall to held-card or XMult scaling that does not destroy its own cards.

situation: Strength is held with a Glass Ten available while Photograph wants a Glass face card in the lead slot.
options: Raise two low cards toward a Straight or a rank build.
Raise the Glass Ten to a Glass Jack for the lead slot.
lesson: Strength changes rank without touching the enhancement, so a Glass Ten becomes a Glass face; the recorded run did exactly this and the next hand scored 2,853,107,712 against a 600,000,000 boss.
reversal: Spend Strength elsewhere when a Glass face already exists or when the rank change breaks a Flush, Straight or held-King plan.

situation: The Tooth is the visible boss and the reserve is small.
options: Enter on the current cash and play five cards every hand.
Bank money in the shop before it and plan fewer, larger hands.
lesson: The Tooth takes $1 per card played, so four hands of five, five, five and one cost $16: the recorded run entered on $6, finished at -$10 and had no money left for the shop it never reached.
reversal: Ignore the drain when the blind falls in one or two hands and the following shop is not part of the plan.

situation: Crimson Heart disables one random Joker every hand while a copier is pointed at the build's single largest multiplier.
options: Keep the highest-expected order and accept the worst case.
Spread the multipliers so no single disable removes two of them.
lesson: Concentration cuts both ways: with Brainstorm copying Photograph the recorded hand fell from 11,548,293 to 180,442 when Photograph was the Joker disabled, against 20x or less for every other slot.
reversal: Keep the concentrated order when it maximises the expected score and the worst disable still clears the blind, as 180,442 did against 100,000 here.

situation: Blueprint and Brainstorm are both owned over a played-card engine that has one retrigger Joker and one multiplier Joker.
options: Point both copiers at the single largest multiplier.
Give Blueprint the retrigger and Brainstorm the multiplier.
lesson: Blueprint copies its right neighbour and Brainstorm the leftmost Joker: the recorded run used five adjacent swaps to sit Blueprint left of Hanging Chad with Photograph leftmost, so retriggers and X2 compounded.
reversal: Copy one Joker twice only when it out-scales the pair, and recheck after every sale because both targets move with the order.

situation: Steel Joker is offered or owned while the deck holds only a few Steel cards.
options: Pass until the deck already holds many Steel cards.
Take it and grow the Steel count with Tarots and packs.
lesson: Steel Joker counts Steel in the whole deck, not the hand: the recorded copy started at two Steel cards and reached nine by Ante 13, while playing a Steel card adds nothing because Steel only pays while held.
reversal: Skip it when the deck cannot gain Steel cheaply, or when the slot is needed by a multiplier that is already larger.

situation: A Negative Tag sits on a still-selectable blind while the Joker slots are already full.
options: Play the blind for its cash and its shop.
Skip for the tag and take the free Negative Joker.
lesson: The recorded Ante 7 skip turned the next base-edition shop Joker into a free Negative Steel Joker, which raised the Joker limit from six to seven instead of competing for a slot.
reversal: Play the blind when its cash and shop matter more, or when no Joker worth a permanent slot is likely to appear in it.

situation: An Investment Tag is on an early small blind whose own cash reward is only a few dollars.
options: Play the small blind for its reward and its shop.
Skip for the tag and collect $25 after the boss.
lesson: The recorded Ante 1 skip paid exactly $25 at the boss cash out, moving money from $5 to $39 in one step and funding the first real shop; the ante target was unchanged.
reversal: Play the blind when the run needs that shop now, or when the boss looks unlikely to fall, because the tag pays nothing until it does.

situation: Endless play continues past Ante 8 with Seed Money owned and a shop offering rerolls and small purchases.
options: Spend down each shop hunting one more upgrade.
Hold $50 and buy only what raises the multiplier engine.
lesson: Interest is the only compounding income: the recorded run let its $50 floor lapse after Ante 7, and its last eight cash outs paid $25 of a possible $80, arriving at Ante 13 with $2.
reversal: Spend below the floor when the purchase is the engine upgrade the next blind actually needs; forgone interest is cheap next to a failed blind.

situation: Observatory is bought late in endless while two copies of the played hand's Planet occupy both consumable slots.
options: Use the Planets for permanent hand levels and free the slots.
Hold both and take X1.5 each on every hand of that family.
lesson: The recorded run spent its last $10 on Observatory and held two Jupiters; the next two Flushes scored 125,384,579,763 and 134,231,931,235, but the full slots then blocked every Tarot in the final shops.
reversal: Use the Planets when the extra levels clear the blind anyway, or when a slot is needed for a deck edit the engine depends on.
